panel: notebook: Under the hood ('How arguments and results travel')
what: The calling-convention sentence applies the x86-64 System V rules to all '64-bit Linux and macOS'. Apple Silicon Macs (and ARM64 Linux) use the AArch64 convention: eight argument registers, with the result in x0/w0, not rax. Also, an int result comes back in eax, the low half of rax.
evidence: ch7.html:1066 "On 64-bit Linux and macOS (the System V convention), the first six whole-number arguments travel in processor registers rather than in memory, and an int result comes back in a register called rax."
fix: 'On x86-64 Linux and Intel Macs (the System V convention) ... an int result comes back in eax (part of rax). ARM64 machines, such as Apple Silicon Macs, use eight argument registers instead.'

panel: notebook: Under the hood ('How can two machines share a name?')
what: The notebook says the return type is left out of the mangled name and that this is why functions can't be overloaded on return type alone. That reverses cause and effect: the language rule (overloads must differ in their parameters) comes first, and the mangling scheme follows it.
evidence: ch7.html:1072 "The return type is not part of the mangled name, which is why two functions that differ only in their return type can't be overloaded."
fix: 'The return type is not part of the mangled name: C++ never chooses an overload by return type, so it doesn't need to be.'
